keyVerseText: For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.
rootMeaning: The root of διχάζω (dicházō) comes from the Greek δίς (dís), meaning 'again' or 'twice,' which conveys the idea of splitting or dividing something into two parts. Literally, it implies a dual division or separation, going beyond the simple English gloss of 'at variance' by emphasizing a clear and deliberate breaking apart into two distinct sides or factions. This etymological insight highlights the intensity and definitiveness of the division implied by the term.
usageInScripture: The word διχάζω appears only once in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'at variance,' which reveals its specialized use to describe a profound and personal division. The singular occurrence suggests that it is employed to mark significant relational or ideological separation rather than casual disagreement. This focused usage underscores the word's strong connotation of alienation or setting apart in conflict.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding διχάζω in its original sense of a decisive division enriches our comprehension of the spiritual and relational conflicts that arise in the Christian life. It reminds believers that following Christ may cause division even among close family members, reflecting the cost of discipleship and the priority of allegiance to Christ above all. This word points to the reality that the gospel can separate those who accept it from those who reject it, emphasizing the seriousness of faith commitments and the transformative power of Christ's message to reorder human relationships.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 10:35, where Jesus says He has come to set a man at variance against his father and a daughter against her mother, the use of διχάζω highlights the profound and intentional nature of this division. It is not mere disagreement but a deep, relational rupture caused by allegiance to Christ. This word captures the cost of discipleship, showing that following Jesus may bring conflict within the most intimate bonds, underscoring the radical call of the gospel to prioritize God's kingdom above all else.
